                                  13            Before the Court is Defendant Natera, Inc.’s motion to dismiss. ECF No. 25. The Court

                                  14   will grant the motion.

                                  15   I.       BACKGROUND

                                  16            Plaintiffs Shannon Petersen and Erin Vedrode bring this lawsuit based on Natera’s

                                  17   allegedly “false, deceptive, unfair, and misleading advertising, marketing, and promotion of [its]

                                  18   preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (‘PGT-A’ or ‘PGT-A testing’),” which Natera

                                  19   markets as Spectrum. ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 1, 74. They seek to represent a nationwide class of

                                  20   consumers, as well as classes of consumers in the states where they reside—California for

                                  21   Petersen and Michigan for Vedrode.

                                  22            The complaint alleges the following:

                                  23                   PGT-A testing is marketed and sold by Defendant as an add-on to
                                                       the IVF [in vitro fertilization] process and purports to screen
                                  24                   embryos for chromosomal abnormalities. With respect to PGT-A
                                                       conducted by Defendant, IVF clinics perform a biopsy and send a
                                  25                   small number of cells from the embryo to Defendant who performs
                                                       the PGT-A testing and provides results to the customer and their
                                  26                   clinic. The results purport to determine which embryos are
                                                       “euploid” or best suited for implantation and which embryos are
                                  27                   “aneuploid” or abnormal and not suited for implantation.
                                  28

                                                      PGT-A testing is marketed and sold by Defendant to people
                                   1                  pursuing IVF as increasing the chance of embryo implantation,
                                                      decreasing the chance of miscarriage, reducing the time to
                                   2                  pregnancy, increasing the rate of pregnancy, increasing live birth
                                                      rates, improving the chance of a healthy pregnancy, and improving
                                   3                  pregnancy rates for all ages, especially those of advanced maternal
                                                      age which Defendant identifies as over 35 years old. Defendant also
                                   4                  markets PGT-A as being 99% accurate. Based on these material
                                                      representations and the material omissions that underlay them as
                                   5                  detailed below, Plaintiffs and Class members choose to purchase
                                                      PGT-A testing from Defendants.
                                   6
                                                      The above representations by Defendant are false and/or misleading
                                   7                  and deceptive based upon the omission of material information.
                                                      Studies show that when looking at clinic pregnancy, miscarriage, or
                                   8                  live-birth rates, there is no difference between cycles utilizing
                                                      PGT-A and cycles not utilizing PGT-A. Studies also show the
                                   9                  accuracy rating for PGT-A is significantly lower than advertised.

                                  12   implantation; Decrease the chance of miscarriage; Reduce the time to pregnancy; and Reduce the

                                  13   chance of having a child with a chromosomal abnormality or single gene condition.” Id. ¶ 185

                                  16   while decreasing the chance of miscarriage or having a child with a genetic condition,” id. ¶ 207;

                                  17   and that “PGT-A and PGT-M can improve the chance of a health pregnancy,” id. ¶ 210.1

                                  22                  chromosomes X and Y).

                                  25   and PGT-A testing with a typical accuracy of greater than 99%,” id. ¶ 193, and it previously

                                  26   stated, “Pregnancy rates are higher when Spectrum is performed with IVF,” id. ¶ 198. The

                                  25   November 2022,” with Petersen having paid $700 and Vedrode having paid $2250 “plus

                                  26   additional costs.” Id. ¶¶ 249–50, 252–53.2 They relied on Natera’s statements “that PGT-A

                                   6          On the basis of the above allegations, Plaintiffs bring claims for: (1) violation of the

                                   7   California Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, et seq., under the

                                   8   unfair and fraudulent prongs; (2) violation of the UCL under the unlawful prong; (3) violation of

                                   9   the California Consumers Legal Remedies Act (“CLRA”), Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1750, et seq.;

                                  10   (4) violation of the Michigan Consumer Protection Act (“MCPA”), Mich. Comp. Laws

                                  11   §§ 445.901, et seq.; (5) breach of the implied warranty of merchantability; (6) breach of the

Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   and (10) unjust enrichment.

                                  14   II.    JURISDICTION

                                  15          The Court has jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(2).

                                  16   III.   LEGAL STANDARD

                                  17          A complaint must contain “a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the

                                  18   pleader is entitled to relief.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a). In addition, a party “alleging fraud or mistake”

                                  19   must “state with particularity the circumstances constituting fraud or mistake.” Fed. R. Civ. P.

                                  20   9(b). Even if “fraud is not a necessary element of a claim”:

                                  21                  the plaintiff may allege a unified course of fraudulent conduct and
                                                      rely entirely on that course of conduct as the basis of a claim. In
                                  22                  that event, the claim is said to be “grounded in fraud” or to “sound
                                                      in fraud,” and the pleading of that claim as a whole must satisfy the
                                  23                  particularity requirement of Rule 9(b).
                                  24   Vess v. Ciba-Geigy Corp. USA, 317 F.3d 1097, 1103–04 (9th Cir. 2003).

                                  25          “Dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) [of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure] is appropriate

                                  26   only where the complaint lacks a cognizable legal theory or sufficient facts to support a cognizable

                                  27   legal theory.” Mendiondo v. Centinela Hosp. Med. Ctr., 521 F.3d 1097, 1104 (9th Cir. 2008).

                                  28   “To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as
                                                                                          4
                                            Case 4:24-cv-07062-JST        Document 47         Filed 08/04/25      Page 5 of 19




                                   1   true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678

                                   2   (2009) (quoting Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)). “A claim has facial

                                   3   plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable

                                   4   inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged.” Id. In determining whether a

                                   5   plaintiff has met this plausibility standard, the Court must “accept all factual allegations in the

                                   6   complaint as true and construe the pleadings in the light most favorable” to the plaintiff. Knievel

                                   7   v. ESPN, 393 F.3d 1068, 1072 (9th Cir. 2005). Dismissal for failure to state a claim should be

                                   8   with leave to amend, “even if no request to amend the pleading was made, unless [the court]

                                   9   determines that the pleading could not possibly be cured by the allegation of other facts.” Cook,

                                  10   Perkiss & Liehe, Inc. v. N. Cal. Collection Serv. Inc., 911 F.2d 242, 247 (9th Cir. 1990) (per

                                  11   curiam).

                                  12   IV.     REQUESTS FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE AND INCORPORATION BY REFERENCE
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           “Generally, district courts may not consider material outside the pleadings when assessing

                                  14   the sufficiency of a complaint under Rule 12(b)(6) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.”

                                  15   Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc., 899 F.3d 988, 998 (9th Cir. 2018). Judicial notice and

                                  16   incorporation by reference are exceptions to this rule.3 Id. The Ninth Circuit has cautioned

                                  17   against the “overuse and improper application” of these exceptions and warned that the “use of

                                  18   extrinsic documents to resolve competing theories against the complaint risks premature

                                  19   dismissals of plausible claims that may turn out to be valid after discovery.” Id.

                                  20           A court may take judicial notice of “a fact that is not subject to reasonable dispute because

                                  21   it: (1) is generally known within the trial court’s territorial jurisdiction or (2) can be accurately and

                                  22   readily determined from sources whose accuracy cannot reasonably be questioned.” Fed. R. Evid.

                                  23   201(b). Although “a court may take judicial notice of matters of public record without converting

                                  24   a motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment,” it “cannot take judicial notice of

                                  25

                                  26   3
                                         Natera argues “that a court may take judicial notice of documents that are incorporated by
                                  27   reference into a complaint” if certain criteria are satisfied. ECF No. 26 at 3. However, judicial
                                       notice and incorporation by reference are separate doctrines. “Both of these procedures permit
                                  28   district courts to consider materials outside a complaint, but each does so for different reasons and
                                       in different ways.” Khoja, 899 F.3d at 998.
                                                                                           5
                                         Case 4:24-cv-07062-JST          Document 47           Filed 08/04/25    Page 6 of 19




                                   1   disputed facts contained in such public records.” Khoja, 899 F.3d at 999 (citation modified).

                                   2          A court may consider a document as incorporated by reference into a complaint “if the

                                   3   plaintiff refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff’s

                                   4   claim.” United States v. Ritchie, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003). “But the mere mention of the

                                   5   existence of a document is insufficient to incorporate the contents of a document,” and

                                   6   incorporation by reference is appropriate only where “the document’s authenticity is not in

                                   7   question and there are no disputed issues as to the document’s relevance.” Coto Settlement v.

                                   8   Eisenberg, 593 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010). In addition, while a court may generally assume

                                   9   the contents of an incorporated document to be true for purposes of a motion to dismiss, “it is

                                  10   improper to assume the truth of an incorporated document if such assumptions only serve to

                                  11   dispute facts stated in a well-pleaded complaint.” Khoja, 899 F.3d at 1003.

                                  12          Natera seeks consideration of three categories of documents outside the complaint: consent
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   forms signed by Plaintiffs to receive PGT-A testing; scientific studies or articles cited in the

                                  14   complaint; and clinical laboratory licenses issued to Natera by the California Department of Public

                                  15   Health. ECF No. 26.

                                  16          A.      Consent Forms

                                  17          First, Natera argues that Plaintiffs’ consent forms are “referenced in Plaintiffs’ complaint

                                  18   as one of the media through which Natera allegedly defrauded them.” ECF No. 26 at 4. Plaintiffs

                                  19   counter that the forms “are barely addressed in Plaintiffs’ Complaint and do not form the basis of

                                  20   the Complaint.” ECF No. 35 at 3. While the complaint does not quote from the consent forms,

                                  21   Plaintiffs’ breach of express warranty and fraud by concealment claims explicitly rely on

                                  22   statements made on those forms. ECF No. 1 ¶ 312 (alleging, as part of breach of express warranty

                                  23   claim, that “Defendant purports, through its marketing and advertising, patient brochure, consent

                                  24   forms, statements, and test results that its PGT-A testing is accurate and reliable, among other

                                  25   things as detailed here” (emphasis added)); id. ¶ 332 (alleging, as part of fraud by concealment

                                  26   claim, that “Defendant had a duty to disclose the truth about PGT-A because, through Defendant’s

                                  27   advertising, marketing, website statements, patient brochures, consent form, and other written

                                  28   statements made to consumers, Defendant made partial representations regarding PGT-A
                                                                                          6
                                         Case 4:24-cv-07062-JST          Document 47          Filed 08/04/25    Page 7 of 19




                                   1   including purported representations concerning its reliability and accuracy, but failed to disclose

                                   2   facts that would have materially qualified those partial representations” (emphasis added)). The

                                   3   complaint therefore incorporates the consent forms by reference. Because Plaintiffs do not

                                   4   challenge the forms’ authenticity, the Court will consider them on this motion to dismiss.

                                   5   However, the Court will not consider the contents of the forms as evidence of the truth of the

                                   6   statements contained therein. Khoja, 899 F.3d at 1003.

                                   7          B.      Studies and Articles

                                   8          Second, Natera asks the Court to consider seven “sources cited in Plaintiffs’ complaint as

                                   9   contradicting Natera’s statements regarding PGT-A.” ECF No. 26 at 4. Plaintiffs do not dispute

                                  10   that they “have incorporated dozens of scholarly articles in the Complaint,” ECF No. 35 at 4, nor

                                  11   do they dispute that these articles include the seven sources cited by Natera. The Court considers

                                  12   the articles as having been incorporated by reference into the complaint but, as discussed below,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   does not interpret these “extrinsic documents to resolve competing theories against the complaint.”

                                  14   Khoja, 899 F.3d at 998.

                                  15          C.      Clinical Laboratory Licenses

                                  16          Finally, Natera asks the Court to take judicial notice of clinical licenses issued by the

                                  17   California Department of Public Health. ECF Nos. 26-11 to 26-15. Plaintiffs do not contest the

                                  18   fact or authenticity of these licenses but argue that they are irrelevant. However, as explained

                                  19   below, the Court finds the licenses relevant to determining whether Plaintiffs’ punitive damages

                                  20   claims may move forward. The Court therefore takes judicial notice of the licenses. See, e.g.,

                                  21   DeHoog v. Anheuser-Busch InBev SA/NV, 899 F.3d 758, 763 n.5 (9th Cir. 2018) (granting

                                  22   “motion to take judicial notice of government documents . . . and undisputed matters of public

                                  23   record”).

                                  24   V.     DISCUSSION

                                  25          A.      Pleading with Specificity

                                  26          Plaintiffs acknowledge that their claims for fraud and fraud by concealment, as well as

                                  27   portions of their UCL claims, “allege fraudulent conduct” are therefore subject to the specific

                                  28   pleading requirements of Rule 9(b). ECF No. 34 at 12. They argue that the rule does not apply to
                                                                                         7
                                         Case 4:24-cv-07062-JST          Document 47         Filed 08/04/25    Page 8 of 19




                                   1   all of their UCL claims because “the UCL prohibits business practices that are (1) unlawful,

                                   2   (2) unfair, or (3) fraudulent,” and they “assert their UCL claims under all three prongs.” Id.

                                   3   (emphasis in original). But Plaintiffs’ argument continues by relying on Natera’s alleged

                                   4   “misleading statements and omissions,” id.—i.e., its allegedly fraudulent conduct—and the Court

                                   5   agrees with Natera that all of Plaintiffs’ UCL claims therefore sound in fraud.

                                   6          Plaintiffs do not make any arguments regarding whether their remaining claims sound in

                                   7   fraud, but the Court’s review of the complaint indicates that they do. For example, Plaintiffs’

                                   8   implied warranty of merchantability claim is based on allegations that “Natera advertises, markets,

                                   9   and promotes that PGT-A testing is substantiated, accurate and reliable” when “it is not.” ECF

                                  10   No. 1 ¶ 295. Similarly, Plaintiffs allege that Natera’s “promises and affirmations of fact about

                                  11   PGT-A testing through its marketing and advertising statements, patient brochure, Consent Form,

                                  12   [and] test results” created “express warranties about accuracy and reliability,” which Natera
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   allegedly breached because “its PGT-A testing is not accurate or reliable.” Id. ¶¶ 310–13.

                                  14   Because all of Plaintiffs’ claims rest on the same alleged “unified course of fraudulent conduct,”

                                  15   the entire complaint sounds in fraud and is subject to Rule 9(b)’s pleading requirements. Vess,

                                  16   317 F.3d at 1103.

                                  17          To comply with Rule 9(b), a complaint “must identify the who, what, when, where, and

                                  18   how of the misconduct charged, as well as what is false or misleading about the purportedly

                                  19   fraudulent statement, and why it is false.” Davidson v. Kimberly-Clark Corp., 889 F.3d 956, 964

                                  20   (9th Cir. 2018) (citation modified). This includes “identify[ing] the allegedly misleading

                                  21   representations that each [Plaintiff] saw and relied upon in deciding to purchase” Spectrum. In re

                                  22   Natera Prenatal Testing Litig., 664 F. Supp. 3d 995, 1006 (N.D. Cal. 2023).

                                  23          Plaintiffs have not satisfied these requirements. The complaint alleges that both Petersen

                                  24   and Vedrode “purchased Defendant’s PGT-A testing in or around November 2022” and identifies

                                  25   categories of allegedly false and misleading statements—“that PGT-A testing is greater than 99%

                                  26   accurate, increases the success of IVF, decreases the chance of miscarriage, leads to a higher

                                  27   chance of pregnancy, reduces the time to pregnancy, and increases the chance of implantation and

                                  28   pregnancy”—on which they allegedly based their purchases. ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 248–49, 251–52.
                                                                                        8

                                   1   However, as Natera correctly observes, the complaint alleges only the approximate dates of

                                   2   purchase and not when Plaintiffs viewed the alleged statements or where they viewed them (e.g.,

                                   3   on the website, in a marketing brochure, or elsewhere). Additionally, Plaintiffs cite to different

                                   4   versions of Natera’s brochure, and the complaint is unclear as to whether all of the alleged

                                   5   statements were in the version available prior to Plaintiffs’ purchases. For example, Plaintiffs cite

                                   6   to an online brochure last visited on July 7, 2023, to support an allegation that Natera “previously

                                   8   but they cite to a version last visited on October 8, 2024, to support their contention that Natera

                                   9   “misleadingly states that its PGT-A testing [is] greater than 99% accurate,” id. ¶ 193 & n.91.

                                  10   Neither of these statements appears in the current version of the brochure available at the cited

                                  11   link, and it is not clear whether they were included in the brochure prior to Plaintiffs’ purchases.

                                  12   https://www.natera.com/resource-library/spectrum/spectrum-pgt-a-patient-brochure/
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   [https://perma.cc/229P-4KSS].

                                  14          Likewise, the complaint cites to Natera’s website as last visited on October 8, 2024, the

                                  15   date the complaint was filed and nearly two years after Plaintiffs allegedly purchased Spectrum,

                                  16   e.g., ECF No. 1 ¶ 185 & n. 89, ¶ 192 & n.90, ¶ 206 & n.102, ¶ 212 & 17, and Plaintiffs do not

                                  17   allege that the cited statements appeared on Natera’s website prior to Plaintiffs’ purchases, or even

                                  18   that Plaintiffs viewed the website prior to purchasing. Also, some of the sources relied on by

                                  19   Plaintiffs to allege that Natera’s statements were false or misleading postdate Plaintiffs’ purchases,

                                  20   which means they cannot support Plaintiffs’ allegations that the alleged statements were false or

                                  21   misleading at the time Plaintiffs might have relied on them. E.g., id. ¶ 204 & n.100, ¶ 211 &

                                  22   n.106, ¶ 222 & n.114, ¶ 227 & n.119.

                                  23          For all of the above reasons, Plaintiffs’ allegations fall short of the heightened pleading

                                  24   required by Rule 9(b), and the Court dismisses Plaintiffs’ claims with leave to amend.

                                  25          B.      Remaining Arguments

                                  26          The Court addresses the remainder of the parties’ arguments to provide guidance to

                                  27   Plaintiffs as they consider whether and, if so, how to amend their complaint. However, the Court

                                   2   Comm’r, 745 F.3d 953, 962 n.8 (9th Cir. 2014) (declining to address argument raised only in

                                   7                  1.      Actionability of Claims

                                   8          Natera argues that the Court should dismiss Plaintiffs’ claims because sources incorporated

                                   9   by reference into the complaint contradict the complaint’s allegations. However, “heeding the

                                  10   Ninth Circuit’s warning in Khoja regarding the overuse of incorporation-by-reference, the Court

                                  11   declines to use these extrinsic documents to resolve competing theories against the complaint and

                                  12   risk premature dismissals of plausible claims that may turn out to be valid after discovery.” Sneed

                                  21   Natera cites a study that “acknowledges the[] potential benefits of PGT-A” as including increased

                                  22   pregnancy rates, ECF No. 25 at 18 (citing ECF No. 26-6 at 15–16), but Natera fails to consider the

                                  24   pregnancy in specific patient groups, such as those with advanced maternal age, is based on post

                                  25   hoc analyses and requires further investigation to establish its validity.” ECF No. 26-6 at 15–16

                                   9   or author draws conclusions from non-fraudulent data, based on accurate descriptions of the data

                                  10   and methodology underlying those conclusions, on subjects about which there is legitimate

Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   ONY where the plaintiff “did not sue [defendants] for publishing an article in a scientific journal”

                                  14   and instead “sought to enjoin statements made in commercial advertisements and directed at

                                  25                  2.      Duty to Disclose

                                  26          Natera also argues that it had no duty to disclose any of the information Plaintiffs contend

                                  27   should have been disclosed. Under California law:

                                  28                  There are four circumstances in which nondisclosure or concealment
                                                                                         11
                                        Case 4:24-cv-07062-JST           Document 47        Filed 08/04/25       Page 12 of 19



                                                      may constitute actionable fraud: (1) when the defendant is in a
                                   1                  fiduciary relationship with the plaintiff; (2) when the defendant had
                                                      exclusive knowledge of material facts not known to the plaintiff;
                                   2                  (3) when the defendant actively conceals a material fact from the
                                                      plaintiff; and (4) when the defendant makes partial representations
                                   3                  but also suppresses some material facts.

                                   5   sufficiently alleges a duty under the fourth circumstance. Plaintiffs allege that Natera made

                                   6   representations regarding Spectrum’s accuracy rates and benefits, but that it failed to disclose that

                                   7   studies “show that when looking at clinic pregnancy, miscarriage, or live-birth rates, there is no

                                   8   difference between cycles utilizing PGT-A and cycles not utilizing PGT-A” and that “the accuracy

                                   9   rating for PGT-A is significantly lower than advertised.” ECF No. 1 ¶ 11; see also id. ¶ 189–90

                                  11   Plaintiffs contend were omitted); id. ¶ 230 (alleging that Natera “claims that embryo biopsy and

                                  12   PGT-A are nearly harmless” but “omits to inform consumers of the fact that damage to embryos

                                  13   caused by biopsy may be the reason for unsuccessful IVF outcomes following PGT-A”). These

                                  14   allegations are sufficient to withstand Natera’s challenge to the pleadings on grounds that it did

                                  15   not have a duty to disclose.

                                  18   which “provides that manufacturers have a duty to warn physicians, but not the physicians’

                                  19   patients, about certain risks accompanying use of their prescription drugs and many medical

                                  20   devices.” Himes v. Somatics, LLC, 16 Cal. 5th 209, 221 (2024). When the doctrine applies:

                                  21                  the manufacturer fulfills its general duty of care owed to the patient
                                                      by providing an adequate warning to the patient’s physician. If the
                                  22                  manufacturer fails to provide an adequate warning to the patient's
                                                      physician, then the patient may sue asserting negligence for breach
                                  23                  of its general duty of care or asserting strict liability for marketing a
                                                      product that has been rendered defective due to the inadequate
                                  24                  warning.
                                  25   Id. at 222.

                                  27   instead work with a healthcare provider to receive the testing. But they correctly observe that this

                                  28   Court has already determined that the learned intermediary doctrine does not apply to consumer
                                                                                         12
                                        Case 4:24-cv-07062-JST           Document 47        Filed 08/04/25      Page 13 of 19




                                   1   fraud claims that are not “simply disguised failure-to-warn claims”:

                                                      should apply to Plaintiffs’ California consumer fraud claims. Natera
                                   3                  cites no cases in which California courts have applied this doctrine
                                                      to consumer protection claims. The two federal district courts that
                                   4                  have applied the learned intermediary doctrine to consumer
                                                      protection claims based its application on the similarities between
                                   5                  the claims before them and products liability failure-to-warn claims.

                                   6                  learned intermediary doctrine should apply to Plaintiffs’ consumer

                                   7                  understand Plaintiffs’ claims as “essentially” failure-to-warn claims.

                                  12                  simply disguised failure-to-warn claims, the learned intermediary
Northern District of California




                                                      doctrine should not apply to Plaintiffs’ California consumer

                                  25          Natera argues that Vedrode’s MCPA claim fails as a matter of law because the MCPA

                                  26   “does not apply to . . . [a] transaction or conduct specifically authorized under laws administered

                                  28   Mich. Comp. Laws § 445.904(1)(a), and Natera has been certified by the United States

                                   1   Department of Health and Human Services through the Clinical Laboratory Improvement

                                   2   Amendments (“CLIA”). However, although Natera provided copies of licenses from the

                                   3   California Department of Public Health, ECF Nos. 26-11 to 26-14, it has not submitted any

                                   4   certifications from the federal government. Natera cites to Plaintiffs’ consent forms, which state,

                                   5   “Spectrum tests have been developed and their performance characteristics determined by the

                                   6   CLIA-certified laboratory performing the test.” E.g., ECF No. 26-2 at 6; ECF No. 26-3 at 3. But

                                   7   this is insufficient because, while the Court considers the consent forms as having been

                                  10   conclude that Natera has been certified by the federal government.

                                  12   apply. The Michigan Supreme Court has described the exemption as “broad” and explained “that
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   the relevant inquiry is not whether the specific misconduct alleged by the plaintiffs is ‘specifically

                                  14   authorized.’ Rather, it is whether the general transaction is specifically authorized by law,

                                  15   regardless of whether the specific misconduct alleged is prohibited.” Smith v. Globe Life Ins. Co.,

                                  16   460 Mich. 446, 465, 466 (1999). Thus, for example, a real estate broker is not exempt from the

                                  17   MCPA for providing allegedly usurious mortgage loans “because the transaction at issue,

                                  19   license.” Id. at 463–64 (citing Att’y Gen. v. Diamond Mortg., 414 Mich. 603, 617 (1982)). That

                                  24   Occupational Code] to be performed only by licensed residential home builders.” Id.

                                  28   category of examinations or procedures which includes such examination or procedure.” To

                                   3   the Secretary.” 42 U.S.C. § 263a(d). Those standards are designed “to assure consistent

                                   4   performance by laboratories issued a certificate under this section of valid and reliable laboratory

                                   6   laboratory that “introduces a test system not subject to FDA clearance or approval (including

                                  10   § 493.1253(b)(2).

                                  11          Vedrode is correct that nothing in the CLIA certification scheme specifically authorizes

Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   not the “general transaction.” Smith, 460 Mich. at 465. Although Plaintiffs “allege that [Natera]

                                  14   . . . made multiple misrepresentations, the fact remains that all of the alleged misconduct occurred

                                  16   human body. Liss, 478 Mich. at 215 n.41 (emphasis in original). As in Liss, the alleged activity

                                  17   can “be performed only by” certified laboratories, which makes the activity “specifically

                                  18   authorized” for purposes of construing the MCPA exemption. Id. at 215. Consequently, assuming

                                  19   Natera is CLIA-certified, the MCPA would not apply to the alleged conduct.

                                  20                  5.      Breach of Warranty

                                  21          Natera next argues that Plaintiffs’ “implied warranty claims should be dismissed because
